cls: Topical antiviral - halogenated thymidine (pyrimidine) nucleoside analogue
pharm: An iodinated deoxyuridine analogue that interferes with viral DNA synthesis, used topically against herpes simplex keratitis and (in some countries) cutaneous herpes
quick: Eye: 0.1% solution 1 drop every hour by day and every 2 h at night, or 0.5% ointment 5 times daily, until healing
Avoid unless essential; teratogenic in animals - limited human data

summary: Idoxuridine is a halogenated thymidine (pyrimidine) nucleoside analogue and one of the first clinically used antivirals, applied topically (as eye drops 0.1% or eye ointment 0.5%, and in some countries as a cutaneous solution) chiefly for herpes simplex keratitis, especially dendritic/epithelial corneal ulcers, and for cutaneous herpes simplex/zoster lesions. It is incorporated into viral (and host) DNA in place of thymidine, producing faulty, non-functional DNA and inhibiting viral replication; it is active only superficially and is not used systemically because of toxicity. Typical ophthalmic regimens are 0.1% solution one drop hourly by day and two-hourly at night, or 0.5% ointment five times daily, continued for a short period after healing. Idoxuridine has been discontinued in the United States and largely superseded by more selective agents (aciclovir, ganciclovir, trifluridine); information here follows EMA/BNF and historical monographs.

Cutaneous herpes simplex and herpes zoster lesions (topical, where marketed)

moa: Idoxuridine is a thymidine analogue in which a methyl group is replaced by iodine. After phosphorylation it is incorporated into DNA in place of thymidine during replication, producing structurally faulty DNA that is more susceptible to breakage and that codes for non-functional proteins, thereby inhibiting replication of DNA viruses such as herpes simplex. Because it is incorporated into both viral and host DNA, it lacks selectivity and is too toxic for systemic use, restricting it to topical (ophthalmic/cutaneous) therapy of superficial herpetic infections.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to idoxuridine or formulation components
Deep stromal/uveal herpetic disease as sole therapy (epithelial agent only)
relative: Concurrent topical corticosteroids without specialist supervision
monitor: Local irritation, follicular conjunctivitis or punctate keratopathy

preg: Idoxuridine has been teratogenic in animal studies and human data are limited. It should be avoided in pregnancy unless considered essential, and then used for the shortest necessary period on the smallest area.
lact: There are limited data; systemic absorption from topical ocular or cutaneous use is minimal, but caution is advised during breastfeeding.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is needed because systemic absorption from topical use is negligible.
hepatic: No specific dosage adjustment is needed because systemic absorption from topical use is negligible.

major: Boric acid-containing eye preparations - may form a precipitate/cause irritation with idoxuridine eye drops; avoid concurrent use
moderate: Topical corticosteroids - may worsen herpetic keratitis; use only under specialist supervision
minor: Other topical ophthalmic agents - separate administration to avoid washout

common: Local irritation, burning or stinging on instillation
serious: Corneal toxicity with prolonged use - punctate or epithelial keratopathy, delayed healing, corneal opacity
rare: Small corneal punctate defects, lid oedema
emergency: Severe allergic/hypersensitivity reaction - discontinue and seek ophthalmic care

monitoring: Local tolerance and signs of toxicity with prolonged use
Therapeutic response within 1-2 weeks; switch agent if no healing

pearls: One of the first antivirals - now largely replaced by more selective agents (aciclovir, ganciclovir, trifluridine) and DISCONTINUED in the US
Incorporated into both viral and host DNA - lacks selectivity, so it is too toxic for systemic use and limited to topical/ophthalmic therapy
Treats epithelial (dendritic) herpetic keratitis; not effective alone for deep stromal disease
Avoid prolonged continuous ocular use (corneal toxicity); do not combine with steroid eye drops unsupervised
NOT FDA-marketed currently - this monograph follows EMA/BNF and historical sources
missed: If you miss a dose of the eye drops/ointment, use it as soon as you remember and then continue the frequent schedule; do not put in extra to catch up. Maintaining frequent dosing matters for effect.
overdose: Topical overdose (extra drops/ointment) is unlikely to cause systemic harm; excess is generally washed out by tears. Local irritation may occur and is managed by rinsing and supportive care. Accidental ingestion of eye preparations should be managed symptomatically with medical advice.
